case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of complex regional pain syndrome presented to the dermatology department for evaluation of a pruritic recurrent rash on her right anterior thigh that started 1 month prior. She had used ice packs to relieve her symptoms. Examination was notable for numerous indurated red nodules and plaques, with erosions over the right anterior thigh (Figure 1A). She reported no similar lesions elsewhere on her body and denied any constitutional symptoms. A skin biopsy was performed from her right thigh (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, indurated plaques and erosions on right anterior thigh. B, Interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary dermal edema, and a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate around adnexal structures and vessels in both the superficial and deep dermis. Overt panniculitis was absent.
case_info.explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrated interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, predominantly located at the basal layer of epidermis. Mild papillary dermal edema and brisk periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis were noted. Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. Patients typically present with pruritic erythematous wheals in areas exposed to cold air, liquids, or objects; lesions appear 5 to 30 minutes after exposure and can last around 30 minutes.8This differs from the current case and cases of ice-pack dermatosis reported in the literature, which describe a more gradual onset and a duration of weeks to months.1-3,9 Histologically, ACU is characterized by mast cell degranulation and perivascular infiltrates, including neutrophils, eosinophils, erythrocytes, monocytes, and fibrin deposition.8ACU could be distinguished from ice-pack dermatosis through a screening cold stimulation test, which involves applying a localized cold object, usually an ice cube, to an unaffected area of the skin for 5 minutes, eliciting a wheal and flare response within 10 minutes that would favor ACU and rule out ice-pack dermatosis.8,10 This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough medical history and clinicopathologic correlation in making a diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. The histologic features of this condition can overlap with those of cold panniculitis, perniosis, and lupus erythematosus.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. Patients typically present with pruritic erythematous wheals in areas exposed to cold air, liquids, or objects; lesions appear 5 to 30 minutes after exposure and can last around 30 minutes.8This differs from the current case and cases of ice-pack dermatosis reported in the literature, which describe a more gradual onset and a duration of weeks to months.1-3,9 Histologically, ACU is characterized by mast cell degranulation and perivascular infiltrates, including neutrophils, eosinophils, erythrocytes, monocytes, and fibrin deposition.8ACU could be distinguished from ice-pack dermatosis through a screening cold stimulation test, which involves applying a localized cold object, usually an ice cube, to an unaffected area of the skin for 5 minutes, eliciting a wheal and flare response within 10 minutes that would favor ACU and rule out ice-pack dermatosis.8,10 This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough medical history and clinicopathologic correlation in making a diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. The histologic features of this condition can overlap with those of cold panniculitis, perniosis, and lupus erythematosus.

   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

B, Interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary dermal edema, and a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate around adnexal structures and vessels in both the superficial and deep dermis. Overt panniculitis was absent.
case_info.explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrated interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, predominantly located at the basal layer of epidermis. Mild papillary dermal edema and brisk periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis were noted. Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. Patients typically present with pruritic erythematous wheals in areas exposed to cold air, liquids, or objects; lesions appear 5 to 30 minutes after exposure and can last around 30 minutes.8This differs from the current case and cases of ice-pack dermatosis reported in the literature, which describe a more gradual onset and a duration of weeks to months.1-3,9 Histologically, ACU is characterized by mast cell degranulation and perivascular infiltrates, including neutrophils, eosinophils, erythrocytes, monocytes, and fibrin deposition.8ACU could be distinguished from ice-pack dermatosis through a screening cold stimulation test, which involves applying a localized cold object, usually an ice cube, to an unaffected area of the skin for 5 minutes, eliciting a wheal and flare response within 10 minutes that would favor ACU and rule out ice-pack dermatosis.8,10 This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough medical history and clinicopathologic correlation in making a diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. The histologic features of this condition can overlap with those of cold panniculitis, perniosis, and lupus erythematosus.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of complex regional pain syndrome presented to the dermatology department for evaluation of a pruritic recurrent rash on her right anterior thigh that started 1 month prior. She had used ice packs to relieve her symptoms. Examination was notable for numerous indurated red nodules and plaques, with erosions over the right anterior thigh (Figure 1A). She reported no similar lesions elsewhere on her body and denied any constitutional symptoms. A skin biopsy was performed from her right thigh (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, indurated plaques and erosions on right anterior thigh. B, Interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary dermal edema, and a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate around adnexal structures and vessels in both the superficial and deep dermis. Overt panniculitis was absent.
case_info.explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrated interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, predominantly located at the basal layer of epidermis. Mild papillary dermal edema and brisk periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis were noted. Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. Patients typically present with pruritic erythematous wheals in areas exposed to cold air, liquids, or objects; lesions appear 5 to 30 minutes after exposure and can last around 30 minutes.8This differs from the current case and cases of ice-pack dermatosis reported in the literature, which describe a more gradual onset and a duration of weeks to months.1-3,9 Histologically, ACU is characterized by mast cell degranulation and perivascular infiltrates, including neutrophils, eosinophils, erythrocytes, monocytes, and fibrin deposition.8ACU could be distinguished from ice-pack dermatosis through a screening cold stimulation test, which involves applying a localized cold object, usually an ice cube, to an unaffected area of the skin for 5 minutes, eliciting a wheal and flare response within 10 minutes that would favor ACU and rule out ice-pack dermatosis.8,10 This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough medical history and clinicopathologic correlation in making a diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. The histologic features of this condition can overlap with those of cold panniculitis, perniosis, and lupus erythematosus.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of complex regional pain syndrome presented to the dermatology department for evaluation of a pruritic recurrent rash on her right anterior thigh that started 1 month prior. She had used ice packs to relieve her symptoms. Examination was notable for numerous indurated red nodules and plaques, with erosions over the right anterior thigh (Figure 1A). She reported no similar lesions elsewhere on her body and denied any constitutional symptoms. A skin biopsy was performed from her right thigh (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, indurated plaques and erosions on right anterior thigh. B, Interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary dermal edema, and a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate around adnexal structures and vessels in both the superficial and deep dermis. Overt panniculitis was absent.
case_info.explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrated interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, predominantly located at the basal layer of epidermis. Mild papillary dermal edema and brisk periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis were noted. Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. Patients typically present with pruritic erythematous wheals in areas exposed to cold air, liquids, or objects; lesions appear 5 to 30 minutes after exposure and can last around 30 minutes.8This differs from the current case and cases of ice-pack dermatosis reported in the literature, which describe a more gradual onset and a duration of weeks to months.1-3,9 Histologically, ACU is characterized by mast cell degranulation and perivascular infiltrates, including neutrophils, eosinophils, erythrocytes, monocytes, and fibrin deposition.8ACU could be distinguished from ice-pack dermatosis through a screening cold stimulation test, which involves applying a localized cold object, usually an ice cube, to an unaffected area of the skin for 5 minutes, eliciting a wheal and flare response within 10 minutes that would favor ACU and rule out ice-pack dermatosis.8,10 This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough medical history and clinicopathologic correlation in making a diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. The histologic features of this condition can overlap with those of cold panniculitis, perniosis, and lupus erythematosus.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of complex regional pain syndrome presented to the dermatology department for evaluation of a pruritic recurrent rash on her right anterior thigh that started 1 month prior. She had used ice packs to relieve her symptoms. Examination was notable for numerous indurated red nodules and plaques, with erosions over the right anterior thigh (Figure 1A). She reported no similar lesions elsewhere on her body and denied any constitutional symptoms. A skin biopsy was performed from her right thigh (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, indurated plaques and erosions on right anterior thigh. B, Interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary dermal edema, and a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate around adnexal structures and vessels in both the superficial and deep dermis. Overt panniculitis was absent.
case_info.explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrated interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, predominantly located at the basal layer of epidermis. Mild papillary dermal edema and brisk periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis were noted. Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of complex regional pain syndrome presented to the dermatology department for evaluation of a pruritic recurrent rash on her right anterior thigh that started 1 month prior. She had used ice packs to relieve her symptoms. Examination was notable for numerous indurated red nodules and plaques, with erosions over the right anterior thigh (Figure 1A). She reported no similar lesions elsewhere on her body and denied any constitutional symptoms. A skin biopsy was performed from her right thigh (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, indurated plaques and erosions on right anterior thigh. B, Interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary dermal edema, and a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate around adnexal structures and vessels in both the superficial and deep dermis. Overt panniculitis was absent.
case_info.explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrated interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, predominantly located at the basal layer of epidermis. Mild papillary dermal edema and brisk periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis were noted. Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. Patients typically present with pruritic erythematous wheals in areas exposed to cold air, liquids, or objects; lesions appear 5 to 30 minutes after exposure and can last around 30 minutes.8This differs from the current case and cases of ice-pack dermatosis reported in the literature, which describe a more gradual onset and a duration of weeks to months.1-3,9 Histologically, ACU is characterized by mast cell degranulation and perivascular infiltrates, including neutrophils, eosinophils, erythrocytes, monocytes, and fibrin deposition.8ACU could be distinguished from ice-pack dermatosis through a screening cold stimulation test, which involves applying a localized cold object, usually an ice cube, to an unaffected area of the skin for 5 minutes, eliciting a wheal and flare response within 10 minutes that would favor ACU and rule out ice-pack dermatosis.8,10 This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough medical history and clinicopathologic correlation in making a diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. The histologic features of this condition can overlap with those of cold panniculitis, perniosis, and lupus erythematosus.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s with a medical history of complex regional pain syndrome presented to the dermatology department for evaluation of a pruritic recurrent rash on her right anterior thigh that started 1 month prior. She had used ice packs to relieve her symptoms. Examination was notable for numerous indurated red nodules and plaques, with erosions over the right anterior thigh (Figure 1A). She reported no similar lesions elsewhere on her body and denied any constitutional symptoms. A skin biopsy was performed from her right thigh (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, indurated plaques and erosions on right anterior thigh. B, Interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, mild papillary dermal edema, and a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate around adnexal structures and vessels in both the superficial and deep dermis. Overt panniculitis was absent.
case_info.explanation: Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrated interface dermatitis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, predominantly located at the basal layer of epidermis. Mild papillary dermal edema and brisk periadnexal and perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis were noted. Rare vessels in the subcutis showed perivascular inflammation, but no overt panniculitis was seen. Increased dermal mucin was observed with Alcian blue stain (Figure 2). CD123 results highlighted occasional small clusters of plasmacytoid dendritic cells in the superficial and deep dermis. The patient admitted to daily application of hot/cold patches across her body, as well as the daily use of ice packs specifically on the affected area. This with the histopathological findings confirmed the diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. Ice-pack dermatosis is an uncommon condition cataloged under cold-induced dermatoses. Most cases reported in the literature involve patients with chronic pain who use ice packs for therapeutic purposes, potentially leading to vasoconstriction and reduced perfusion in areas where lesions develop. The typical presentation includes painful erythematous purpuric papules and plaques with ulceration on the lower back or buttocks.1,2Histopathological examination is challenging, as it shares similarities with cold panniculitis, perniosis, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE).3Treatment consists of avoidance of ice-pack use. The clinical picture of the present patient could be similar to that of lupus erythematosus panniculitis in that it manifests as tender erythematous subcutaneous indurated nodules or plaques. However, it can affect the face, arms, buttocks, and thighs, and this patient only had lesions on her right thigh.4,5Common histopathological findings between CLE and ice-pack dermatosis include perivascular and perieccrine infiltrates, increased dermal mucin, and vacuolar interface changes with necrotic keratinocytes. CLE typically exhibits larger clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In contrast, the present patient also had small clusters of CD123-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, consistent with findings of the ice-pack dermatosis case series reported by West et al.3 Cold panniculitis and perniosis are the most prevalent cold-induced dermatologic disorders. Cold panniculitis manifests as indurated and erythematous nodules and plaques at sites exposed to cold and wet conditions. While it is more frequent in infants, adult cases affecting the thighs of equestrians and cold-therapy device users have been documented.6Cold panniculitis is characterized by lobular panniculitis, predominantly composed of lymphocytes. Neutrophilic infiltrates or granulomas may be present. Typically, the dermis shows a deep perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and inflammation is most intense at the dermal-subcutaneous junction. Fat necrosis with foamy macrophages is evident.3,7Even though the present patient had a lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the deep dermis, there was no overt panniculitis. Moreover, an important difference between ice-pack dermatosis and cold panniculitis is that the latter lacks vacuolar change as well as papillary dermal edema.7 Acquired cold urticaria (ACU) is one of the most frequent forms of physical urticaria, predominantly affecting young adults. It can be idiopathic or secondary to various conditions such as infections, cryoglobulinemias, or cancers. Clinical manifestations of ACU vary from localized skin reactions triggered by cold stimuli to systemic reactions that may progress to anaphylaxis. Patients typically present with pruritic erythematous wheals in areas exposed to cold air, liquids, or objects; lesions appear 5 to 30 minutes after exposure and can last around 30 minutes.8This differs from the current case and cases of ice-pack dermatosis reported in the literature, which describe a more gradual onset and a duration of weeks to months.1-3,9 Histologically, ACU is characterized by mast cell degranulation and perivascular infiltrates, including neutrophils, eosinophils, erythrocytes, monocytes, and fibrin deposition.8ACU could be distinguished from ice-pack dermatosis through a screening cold stimulation test, which involves applying a localized cold object, usually an ice cube, to an unaffected area of the skin for 5 minutes, eliciting a wheal and flare response within 10 minutes that would favor ACU and rule out ice-pack dermatosis.8,10 This case highlights the importance of obtaining a thorough medical history and clinicopathologic correlation in making a diagnosis of ice-pack dermatosis. The histologic features of this condition can overlap with those of cold panniculitis, perniosis, and lupus erythematosus.
